title: Structuralism and Postmodernism: Foucault, Derrida and Lyotard
subtitle: Structures of meaning, webs of power and the end of grand stories
objectives: By the end you will be able to explain Saussure's account of the sign and why meaning depends on differences within a system.
By the end you will be able to describe how structuralism spread from linguistics to anthropology and culture.
By the end you will be able to explain Foucault's ideas of power/knowledge, discipline and the panopticon.
By the end you will be able to describe Derrida's deconstruction and Lyotard's incredulity toward metanarratives.
By the end you will be able to state the main criticisms of postmodern thought and the replies to them.
hook:
Why does the word *cat* mean a small furry animal? There is nothing cat-like about the sound. In French the same creature is *chat*, in Japanese *neko*. Now a harder question: why does the colour red mean *stop* on a traffic light? Not because red is naturally stoppy, but because it stands in a system against green and amber. Change the system and the meaning changes.

From this simple observation about language grew one of the most ambitious and controversial movements in twentieth-century thought. First, **structuralism** claimed that meaning everywhere, in language, myths, kinship, fashion and food, comes from hidden structures of difference. Then a generation of French thinkers, often grouped as **post-structuralists** or **postmodernists**, turned the method against itself, asking how such structures are tied to power, how they can never fully fix meaning, and whether any grand story can explain them all. Their ideas transformed literary studies, history and the social sciences, and provoked some of the angriest disputes in modern philosophy.

sections.heading: Saussure: Language as a System of Differences
sections.body:
Ferdinand de Saussure (1857–1913) was a Swiss linguist who taught at the University of Geneva. He never wrote the book that made him famous. After his death, two colleagues, Charles Bally and Albert Sechehaye, compiled his lectures from students' notes and published them as the *Course in General Linguistics* (1916).

Saussure analysed language as a system of **signs**. Each sign has two sides, like two sides of a sheet of paper: the **signifier** (the sound-image, such as the sound *tree*) and the **signified** (the concept of a tree). The link between them is **arbitrary**: nothing about the sound *tree* resembles trees, which is why different languages use different words.

His deeper insight was that a sign gets its value not from any connection to things but from its differences from other signs in the system. *Cat* means what it means partly because it is not *bat*, *cap* or *dog*. Saussure put it boldly: in language there are only differences without positive terms. Compare chess: a knight is defined not by its material or shape (you could replace a lost knight with a coin) but by the moves it can make relative to other pieces.

Saussure also distinguished **langue**, the shared system of rules that makes speech possible, from **parole**, individual acts of speaking. And he distinguished studying language at one moment in time (synchronic) from studying its historical change (diachronic). Linguists before him had mostly traced word histories; Saussure insisted on studying the system as it works now.

Compare Wittgenstein's later view that meaning is use within language games (Day 73). Both moved away from the idea that words get meaning by simply naming objects. Saussure stressed system and difference; Wittgenstein stressed practice and use.

sections.heading: Structuralism Spreads
sections.body:
In the 1950s and 1960s, French thinkers applied Saussure's method far beyond language. The idea was that human cultures are full of sign systems whose meanings depend on hidden structures that the people using them are usually unaware of.

The anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss (1908–2009) analysed kinship systems and myths from around the world. He argued that myths from very different cultures share deep structures, often built on **binary oppositions**, such as raw and cooked, nature and culture, life and death, which the myths try to mediate. Beneath the bewildering variety of human cultures, he thought, lie universal structures of the human mind.

The critic Roland Barthes (1915–1980), in *Mythologies* (1957), turned the method on everyday French culture: wrestling matches, soap powder advertisements, steak and chips, the new Citroën car. His most famous example was a magazine cover showing a young Black soldier in French uniform saluting, eyes raised, presumably to the French flag. On the surface it is just a photograph. At a second level, Barthes argued, it conveys a **myth**: that France is a great empire whose subjects, whatever their colour, serve it faithfully, so there is nothing wrong with colonialism. Myth, for Barthes, turns history into nature, making contingent arrangements look obvious and eternal.

Structuralism had a radical implication. If meaning comes from structures we do not control, then the individual subject, the free, self-aware chooser celebrated by Sartre (Day 77), is not the master of meaning but more like a product of the systems it speaks through. Structuralists spoke, provocatively, of the death of the subject or the death of the author. This was a direct challenge to existentialism, and by the mid-1960s structuralism had replaced it as the leading intellectual fashion in Paris.

sections.heading: Foucault: Power, Knowledge and the Panopticon
sections.body:
Michel Foucault (1926–1984) is often called a post-structuralist, though he rejected every label. He was a historian of ideas who studied how institutions and forms of knowledge, about madness, illness, crime and sexuality, came to shape how people understand themselves.

In his *History of Madness* (1961) he argued that the way Europe separated the mad from the sane and confined them was not simply scientific progress but a historical change in how reason defined its others. In *The Order of Things* (1966) he argued that each era has an underlying system of knowledge, which he called an **episteme**, setting the conditions for what can count as true. The book ends with the famous image that “man”, as an object of the human sciences, is a recent invention that might one day be erased, like a face drawn in sand at the edge of the sea.

His most influential book is *Discipline and Punish* (1975). It opens with a horrific account of the public torture and execution of Robert-François Damiens in Paris in 1757, for attempting to kill the king. Then it jumps forward some eighty years to a prison timetable: a minute-by-minute schedule of waking, praying, working and sleeping. Within less than a century, punishment had changed from spectacular violence on the body to quiet regulation of time, behaviour and soul. Was this progress? Foucault suggests it was also a new, more efficient form of power.

The symbol of this new power is the **panopticon**, a prison design proposed by Jeremy Bentham, whom you met as the founder of utilitarianism (Day 61). Cells are arranged in a ring around a central watchtower. Each prisoner can be seen at any moment but cannot see whether anyone is in the tower. So he must behave as if he is always watched, and eventually he watches himself. Power no longer needs chains; it works through visibility and self-discipline.

Foucault saw this **disciplinary power** spreading through schools, barracks, hospitals and factories: timetables, examinations, rankings, records and norms that produce **docile bodies**, useful and obedient. He also coined the term **power/knowledge**: power and knowledge are bound together. Knowledge about people, such as psychiatric categories, school reports and crime statistics, gives institutions power over them, and power creates new fields of knowledge. Crucially, Foucault thought power is not only repressive, a king saying no. It is **productive**: it produces identities, categories, desires and norms, and it circulates everywhere, through countless small practices rather than from a single centre.

Foucault was also active politically, campaigning on prison conditions in the 1970s. He died in 1984 of an AIDS-related illness, while still working on his multi-volume *History of Sexuality*.

sections.heading: Derrida: Deconstruction
sections.body:
Jacques Derrida (1930–2004) was born into a Jewish family in El Biar, near Algiers, and as a boy was expelled from school under the antisemitic laws of Vichy France. In 1967 he published three books, including *Of Grammatology*, which launched the method called **deconstruction**.

Derrida accepted Saussure's insight that meaning comes from differences, then pushed it further. If every sign means what it does only through its differences from other signs, which in turn depend on further differences, then meaning is never fully present in any single word or moment. It is always deferred along a chain. Derrida coined the word **différance**, which in French sounds identical to *différence*, the difference being visible only in writing, to name this double movement of differing and deferring.

He argued that Western philosophy, since Plato (Day 11), has been driven by a desire for presence: a final meaning, truth or foundation fully present to the mind. He called this **logocentrism**. It shows up in **hierarchical binary oppositions**: speech over writing, presence over absence, mind over body, nature over culture, male over female. In each pair, the first term is treated as original and pure, the second as secondary or corrupt.

Deconstruction is a way of reading texts closely to show how these hierarchies undermine themselves. Derrida's most famous example: philosophers from Plato to Rousseau (Day 53) treated writing as a mere copy of speech, which was supposedly closer to living thought. Yet they kept describing speech and thought using metaphors of writing, inscriptions on the soul and so on. The supposedly secondary term turns out to be built into the primary one.

Deconstruction is not simply destruction, and it is not a claim that texts mean anything you like. Derrida read with fierce attention to detail. His notorious phrase *there is nothing outside the text* is often taken to mean that the real world does not exist. Derrida later explained that he meant that there is no access to anything without context, interpretation and systems of difference. Critics remain unconvinced that this is so modest.

In 1992 a proposal to give Derrida an honorary degree at Cambridge University provoked a public letter of protest from a group of philosophers, including W. V. O. Quine (Day 74), accusing his work of obscurity. The university voted in favour of the degree.

sections.heading: Lyotard and the Postmodern Condition
sections.body:
The word **postmodernism** was popularised in philosophy by Jean-François Lyotard (1924–1998). In the late 1970s the Council of Universities of the Quebec government commissioned him to write a report on knowledge in the most advanced societies. The result was *The Postmodern Condition: A Report on Knowledge*.

Modern societies, Lyotard argued, justified their institutions and knowledge by appeal to grand stories, which he called **metanarratives** or grand narratives. Examples include the Enlightenment story of reason gradually emancipating humanity (Day 57); Hegel's story of Spirit coming to know itself through history (Day 59); and Marx's story of class struggle ending in a classless society (Day 63). These stories gave everything a place and a direction.

Lyotard famously defined the postmodern as **incredulity toward metanarratives**. After the world wars, the Holocaust and the failure of communism, many people no longer believed in any single story of progress that could legitimate all knowledge and politics. Instead there are many local, partial language games (borrowing Wittgenstein's term from Day 73), each with its own rules: science, law, art, ethics, everyday talk.

What fills the vacuum? Lyotard warned that knowledge was increasingly legitimated by **performativity**, the efficiency of a system: does it work, does it pay, does it produce output? Universities would be judged by their usefulness, and knowledge would become a commodity, stored and sold as information. Writing in 1979, he anticipated computerised societies in which whoever controls data controls power. His preferred alternative was a respect for difference and disagreement, a plurality of small narratives rather than imposed consensus.

sections.heading: Criticisms and Replies
sections.body:
Postmodern thought has been fiercely criticised, sometimes fairly and sometimes as a caricature.

- **Self-refutation.** If there are no grand narratives, is that not itself a grand narrative about history? If all knowledge is bound up with power, is Foucault's own history just another power play? Critics see a performative contradiction here, similar to the problem facing the verification principle (Day 71).
- **Relativism.** If meaning is endlessly deferred and truth is tied to power, how can we say that some claims, about climate, history or medicine, are simply true? The worry is that these ideas undermine the very facts needed to criticise injustice.
- **Obscurity.** Critics, including John Searle, who debated Derrida in the 1970s over Austin's theory of speech acts (Day 73), accused him of wilful vagueness. In 1996 the physicist Alan Sokal had a deliberately nonsensical parody article, full of postmodern jargon about physics, accepted by the journal *Social Text*, which many took as a sign of lax standards.
- **Politics without norms.** Jürgen Habermas (Day 80), in *The Philosophical Discourse of Modernity* (1985), argued that Foucault and Derrida undercut the standards of reason needed for any critique of domination. In a famous 1971 televised debate, Noam Chomsky defended a universal human nature and ideals of justice, while Foucault suggested such ideals were themselves products of particular societies.

Defenders reply that these thinkers are rarely as relativist as their critics claim. Foucault said he was not claiming everything is bad, but that everything is dangerous, so we must always be vigilant. Derrida insisted that deconstruction was driven by a concern for justice. And their tools have proved practically useful: historians of medicine, criminologists, feminists and postcolonial scholars use Foucault to show how categories once thought natural were made, and therefore could be changed, a lesson you will meet again on Day 86.

modernConnection.title: Living in the Panopticon: Smartphones, Workplace Tracking and Self-Surveillance
modernConnection.body:
Foucault's panopticon was an eighteenth-century prison design, but today it can feel like a description of daily life. Smartphones log our locations; websites track what we click; workplaces use software to monitor keystrokes, delivery times and break lengths; doorbell cameras and CCTV cover streets. The scholar Shoshana Zuboff, in *The Age of Surveillance Capitalism* (2019), argued that technology companies profit by collecting behavioural data to predict and shape what we will do.

Foucault's key insight was that the panopticon works even when nobody is in the tower. Because you might be watched, you watch yourself. Think of how people edit what they post, knowing a future employer might look; of students who self-censor in recorded classes; of the quiet pressure of public metrics: likes, follower counts, step counts, productivity scores, ratings for drivers and couriers. Self-tracking apps turn us into both prisoner and guard, constantly measuring ourselves against a norm. That is disciplinary power in Foucault's sense: productive, not merely repressive. It shapes who we become.

Power/knowledge appears too. Data about us, credit scores, risk profiles, algorithmic predictions, gives institutions the power to classify us, and their classifications become facts about our lives: whether we get a loan, an interview, a lower insurance premium.

But be careful. Foucault's analysis can make all monitoring look sinister, when some surveillance serves clear goods: food safety inspections, monitoring of patients in intensive care, cameras that deter violent crime. Democracies also have tools Foucault sometimes underplayed: laws such as the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation, courts, a free press. And the postmodern side of this lesson has its own modern controversy: some writers argue that suspicion of all grand narratives helped prepare the ground for a post-truth politics in which facts are dismissed as power plays; others say this blames philosophers for problems with very different causes. Both debates show these ideas still matter.

vocabulary.definition: A mid-twentieth-century movement holding that meaning in language and culture comes from underlying structures of relations and differences, not from individual elements or the intentions of speakers.
vocabulary.example: A structuralist reading of fairy tales looks for the same pattern of oppositions, such as home and forest, in hundreds of stories.

vocabulary.definition: Saussure's two sides of a linguistic sign: the signifier is the sound or written form, the signified is the concept it expresses.
vocabulary.example: The letters *t-r-e-e* are the signifier; the idea of a tree is the signified.

vocabulary.definition: Foucault's term for the intertwining of power and knowledge: knowledge about people gives institutions power over them, and power creates new forms of knowledge.
vocabulary.example: A psychiatric diagnosis is power/knowledge: a body of knowledge that also authorises treatment, confinement or exemption.

vocabulary.definition: Bentham's design for a prison in which inmates can always be watched from a central tower without knowing when; Foucault used it as a symbol of modern disciplinary power and self-surveillance.
vocabulary.example: An open-plan office where the manager's glass room overlooks every desk works a little like a panopticon.

vocabulary.definition: Foucault's term for modern power that works through surveillance, timetables, examinations and norms to shape useful, obedient individuals, rather than through spectacular punishment.
vocabulary.example: School report cards, rankings and timetables are tools of disciplinary power.

vocabulary.definition: Derrida's method of close reading that shows how a text's hierarchical oppositions, such as speech over writing, undermine themselves and how meaning is never fully fixed.
vocabulary.example: A deconstructive reading might show how a text praising nature over culture relies on cultural assumptions at every step.

vocabulary.definition: A grand story that claims to explain and legitimate all of history or knowledge, such as the story of inevitable progress through reason or the triumph of the working class.
vocabulary.example: The belief that science and technology will inevitably make humanity freer and happier is a metanarrative of progress.

vocabulary.definition: A broad late-twentieth-century outlook, defined by Lyotard as incredulity toward metanarratives, emphasising plurality, difference and scepticism about universal foundations.
vocabulary.example: A postmodern novel might mix genres, tell the same events from conflicting viewpoints and refuse a single true version.

thinkingExercise.title: Watching the Watchers, Reading the Myths
thinkingExercise.prompt: Apply the tools of structuralism and Foucault to your own life, and then test whether postmodern scepticism goes too far.
steps: Pick an advertisement, magazine cover or social media post. Like Barthes, describe its literal content, then the myth it conveys. What does it present as natural that is actually historical?
List three ways you are watched or measured in an ordinary week. For each, ask: do I change my behaviour even when I am not sure anyone is looking?
Choose one category used to classify people (a diagnosis, a grade, a credit score). What power does knowledge in that category give to whom?
Name one grand narrative you believe in, about progress, history, science or your own life. What would it mean to be incredulous toward it?
Write a paragraph: are there some truths that are not merely products of power? How would you defend them against a thoroughgoing postmodernist?

summary: Saussure argued that a sign joins a signifier to a signified arbitrarily, and that meaning comes from differences within a system of signs.
Structuralists such as Lévi-Strauss and Barthes applied this method to myths, kinship and everyday culture, challenging the existentialist idea of the free, self-transparent subject.
Foucault showed how modern disciplinary power works through surveillance, norms and knowledge; the panopticon symbolises power that makes people watch themselves.
Derrida's deconstruction exposes hierarchical oppositions in texts and argues that meaning is always deferred; Lyotard defined the postmodern as incredulity toward metanarratives.
Critics charge postmodern thought with self-refutation, relativism and obscurity; defenders reply that it is a vigilant tool for exposing how supposedly natural categories were made.

quiz.question: According to Saussure, why does a sign like *cat* have the meaning it does?
options: Because its sound naturally resembles the animal
Because of its differences from other signs within the language system
Because an ancient authority assigned it
Because each speaker privately decides what it means
quiz.explanation: The link between signifier and signified is arbitrary, and a sign's value comes from its differences from other signs in the system.

quiz.question: Saussure wrote the *Course in General Linguistics* himself and published it in 1916.
quiz.explanation: It was compiled after his death by his colleagues Bally and Sechehaye from students' lecture notes.

quiz.question: In Barthes's analysis of the magazine cover showing a Black soldier saluting, what is the myth conveyed?
options: That soldiers should always obey orders
That photography is a form of art
That France is a great, fair empire whose subjects serve it loyally, making colonialism seem natural
That magazines should not show military images
quiz.explanation: Barthes argued the image carries a second-level meaning that naturalises French colonialism.

quiz.question: What is the key feature of the panopticon that interested Foucault?
options: Prisoners can see each other at all times
Prisoners are kept in total darkness
Guards must punish prisoners publicly
Prisoners can be watched at any moment without knowing when, so they discipline themselves
quiz.explanation: Uncertain, constant visibility makes inmates internalise the watcher's gaze; power works without chains.

quiz.question: A delivery app ranks couriers by speed and customer ratings, and couriers push themselves harder even when no manager is present. Which concept fits best?
options: Disciplinary power
Différance
Incredulity toward metanarratives
The arbitrariness of the sign
quiz.explanation: Metrics, rankings and visibility produce self-disciplining, useful workers: Foucault's disciplinary power.

quiz.question: Foucault held that power is not only repressive but also productive, creating identities, categories and norms.
quiz.explanation: For Foucault power circulates through many practices and produces knowledge and subjects, rather than simply saying no.

quiz.question: What does Derrida mean by logocentrism?
options: A preference for using logos in advertising
Philosophy's longing for a meaning or truth fully present to the mind, expressed in hierarchies like speech over writing
The study of logic in ancient Greece
The view that language has no relation to thought
quiz.explanation: Derrida argued Western philosophy privileges presence and builds hierarchical oppositions that deconstruction exposes.

quiz.question: How did Lyotard define the postmodern?
options: As the era after 2000
As a style of architecture only
As a belief that all opinions are equally true
As incredulity toward metanarratives
quiz.explanation: In *The Postmodern Condition* (1979) he defined it as disbelief in grand stories that claim to legitimate all knowledge and history.

quiz.question: In the Sokal affair, a physicist had a deliberately nonsensical parody article accepted by the journal *Social Text*.
quiz.explanation: In 1996 Alan Sokal's hoax article was published, and critics took it as evidence of lax standards in some postmodern scholarship.

quiz.question: Which is the self-refutation objection to Lyotard?
options: Saying there are no valid grand narratives seems itself to be a grand narrative about history
Lyotard wrote too many books
Lyotard was not a trained physicist
Lyotard believed in Marxism all his life
quiz.explanation: Critics argue that announcing the end of grand stories is itself a sweeping story about the course of history.

goDeeper.body:
Three debates show these thinkers at their most interesting. The first is the **Searle–Derrida exchange**. Derrida wrote an essay on J. L. Austin's speech-act theory (Day 73), arguing that any utterance can be quoted, repeated and transplanted into new contexts, so that no context can fully fix its meaning. Searle replied in 1977 that Derrida had misread Austin and confused trivial points with deep ones; Derrida answered in a long, mocking essay, later collected in *Limited Inc*. The exchange is often taken as a symbol of the breakdown in communication between analytic and continental philosophy, the split you have followed since Days 69 and 75.

The second is **Foucault's later turn**. In his final years he moved from power to the self: how people in antiquity shaped their own lives through practices of self-care. He studied the Stoics and Epicureans (Days 24–26), and the classicist Pierre Hadot's work on philosophy as a way of life influenced him. Some readers see this as a correction of his earlier picture of subjects produced by power; others see continuity. Either way it brings the course full circle to the Hellenistic ideal of philosophy as therapy and self-transformation.

The third is the **post-truth debate**. Philosophers such as Lee McIntyre in *Post-Truth* (2018) have suggested that postmodern ideas, filtered through popular culture, gave cover to science denial and political disinformation. Others reply that the main causes are economic interests, partisan media and technology, and that Foucault's insistence that knowledge is tied to power is exactly what alerts us to well-funded campaigns of doubt about tobacco or climate. Whose explanation do you find more convincing?

questions: Is it possible to criticise power without appealing to universal standards of truth or justice?
Which grand narratives, if any, do you think we still need?
Does knowing that you are being watched change who you are, or only how you act?
